Do heterogeneous graph neural networks improve cross-cohort glioma grading?

A TCGA–CGGA benchmark with graph ablation and explainability

Abstract · In brief

Glioma grading models can perform strongly within one cohort yet fail to generalize across independent populations. This study benchmarks seven heterogeneous graph neural network architectures using genomic mutation and clinical features, training and selecting models on TCGA and evaluating transfer to CGGA. The graph represents patients and genes as distinct node types, connected through mutation links and patient–patient and gene–gene topology. Across four class-balancing strategies, GNNs were compared with tuned tabular and compact linear baselines, with graph ablation and complementary explainability analyses. The main finding is that graph structure offers useful relational interpretation, especially through gene–patient mutation links, but does not provide a consistent predictive advantage over strong simpler models; external-cohort generalization remains difficult.

02 · Research problem & motivation

Why cross-cohort testing matters
Problem 1

Internal scores can mislead

A model can learn cohort-specific mutation frequencies, age distributions or annotation patterns that do not transfer to another population.

Problem 2

Flat tables hide relationships

Tabular models treat patients as separate rows; a heterogeneous graph can represent shared mutations and co-occurrence relations explicitly.

Research question

Does graph structure help?

The study tests predictive and interpretability value against strong tabular and linear baselines, rather than assuming graph complexity is beneficial.

The target is a binary historical-grade proxy: TCGA LGG vs GBM; CGGA WHO II/III vs WHO IV. It is not a replacement for WHO 2021 integrated molecular diagnosis.

05 · Heterogeneous graph construction

Two node types · four relation types
Gene → Patient (mutates) Patient → Gene (mutated_by) Patient ↔ Patient (BA) Gene ↔ Gene (BA)

Schematic, not a literal rendering of all graph edges. Each cohort is a separate graph. The base bipartite layer links every gene to patients carrying that mutation in both directions; additional Patient–Patient and Gene–Gene layers use Barabási–Albert preferential attachment. The final TCGA training graph contained 1,533 Gene–Patient bipartite edges, 1,335 Patient–Patient BA edges and 37 Gene–Gene BA edges.

06 · MOGAT model architecture

Dual-stream graph + clinical fusion

The diagram below follows the MOGAT description in Section 3.4 of the paper: gene–gene GCN pre-enrichment and Gene–Patient GATv2 form the genomic stream; a two-layer MLP forms the clinical stream; a learned soft fusion gate combines the patient representations; a final GCN aggregates Patient–Patient co-occurrence edges before patient-level classification.

Genomic pathway

Gene identity vectors are first enriched over Gene–Gene BA edges by GCN, then GATv2 propagates mutation-linked information across the bipartite Gene–Patient edges.

Clinical pathway

The 6-dimensional patient clinical representation is processed independently by a two-layer MLP.

Fusion + patient context

A learned soft gate combines per-patient genomic and clinical representations; a final GCN aggregates Patient–Patient co-occurrence signals before binary classification.

Architecture scope: this is the MOGAT variant described in the paper, not a generic multi-omics MOGAT diagram. The paper does not specify a separate named activation, hidden width, dropout, or classifier-head depth for this schematic; none are added here. MOGAT's output is a patient-level binary grade prediction.

07 · Experimental setup & model comparison

Controlled benchmark design

Training & optimization

TCGA only for development: stratified 80/20 train–test split; 5-fold stratified CV on the development partition.

Optuna TPE: 30 trials, seed 42, validation AUC-ROC objective; early stopping patience 20; up to 200 epochs.

Optimization: AdamW, cosine annealing to 5% of initial learning rate; focal loss with inverse-frequency class weights.

Threshold: mean of five fold-wise G-mean-optimal thresholds; transferred unchanged to test and CGGA.

Comparison framework

Heterogeneous GNNs7 × 4

HeteroGATv2 · MOGAT · HyperTMO · RGCN · VEGN · FastHGTConv · SGNN; evaluated with no balancing, SMOTE, CTGAN and ROS.

Tabular classifiers6

XGBoost · Random Forest · SVM · two-hidden-layer MLP · logistic regression · elastic net.

Additional comparators3

IDH1-only logistic regression, IDH1 + age logistic regression, and homogeneous GCN.

Evaluation & statistical validation

Primary metric: AUC-ROC. Secondary metrics: accuracy, precision, Grade-1 recall, Grade-0 recall and F1. The paper reports 10,000 stratified bootstrap resamples for 95% CIs, DeLong AUC testing, McNemar paired prediction tests with Bonferroni correction across 21 pairs, and Spearman correlation between TCGA CV rank and CGGA AUC.

CGGA was kept separate at graph level: no TCGA nodes were included and CGGA labels were not used to construct its edges. Inference was transductive over the full 284-patient CGGA graph; single-patient inference was not evaluated.

Interpretation: gene–patient mutation connectivity is the essential structural signal. Patient–patient BA topology may encode TCGA-specific structure and hinder transfer; gene–gene edges had negligible marginal effect in this ablation.

10 · Explainability findings

Graph-native XAI + tabular SHAP

Consistent biological signals

IDH1

Mutation status

IDH2

Mutation status

Age

At diagnosis

Across graph-native attribution and tabular SHAP, IDH1, IDH2 and age_at_diagnosis recur as major predictors. Feature importance is associative, not causal.

Grade-specific patterns

TCGA Grade 0: MOGAT attention was highest for IDH1 (0.4149).

TCGA Grade 1: EGFR (0.1986) and PTEN (0.1368) received higher attention.

Clinical signal: age at diagnosis remained the leading clinical feature in both cohorts.

Interpretation caution

The CGGA RGCN explainability ranking elevated GRIN2A, but it is mutated in only 1 of 284 patients (0.4%); the paper explicitly treats this as a single-patient artifact, not a biological conclusion. The five graph-native approaches were edge occlusion, integrated gradients, grade-stratified attention, attention entropy and cross-pipeline consensus; tabular baselines were interpreted with SHAP.

11 · Limitations & central conclusion

What the evidence does—and does not—show
Data scope

Restricted feature panel

Only 20 binary mutation flags and three clinical variables; richer expression, methylation and copy-number data were not included.

External evidence

One external cohort

CGGA is the only external cohort. Its population and label definitions differ from TCGA, confounding population shift with label shift.

Method constraints

Exploratory benchmark

Single random seed, standard (not nested/repeated) 5-fold CV, no calibration or decision-curve analysis, and transductive CGGA inference.

Tuning caveat

CGGA not perfectly untouched

The 30-trial HPO budget was informed by preliminary CGGA performance, acknowledged by the authors as a limitation.

Clinical scope

Not deployment-ready

No prospective clinical cohort or deployment setting was evaluated; further validation and calibration are needed.

Label definition

Binary simplification

Historical LGG/GBM and WHO II/III/IV mappings are coarse proxies, not WHO 2021 integrated diagnoses.

Central conclusion

Heterogeneous graphs add structural insight—not a consistent accuracy advantage.

Gene–patient mutation links carry the most useful graph signal, and graph-native explanations expose patient- and grade-specific relationships. Yet strong tabular and compact linear baselines match or exceed the GNNs, while cross-cohort generalization remains a major challenge. The findings support an interpretable benchmarking framework, not clinical readiness.
